name: Cue-dependent forgetting
statement: Much of what looks like forgetting is failure of retrieval rather than loss of the trace, and the right cue brings the item back.
meaning: Two accounts of forgetting have been available for as long as anyone has studied it. Tulving calls one trace-dependent: the stored record decays, deteriorates or is displaced, and the information it held is gone. He calls the other cue-dependent: the record is intact and the cognitive environment at the moment of remembering no longer contains what is needed to reach it. The second account makes a testable move that the first does not. If forgetting is loss, changing the retrieval environment after the failure should not help. If forgetting is inaccessibility, restoring the missing information should reverse it. Tulving's programme is a series of experiments that do exactly that, in free recall, in retroactive interference, and in recognition. The general principle behind them is encoding specificity, stated by Tulving and Thomson as the claim that the memory trace of an event, and hence which retrieval cues will work, are set by the specific encoding operations the system performed on the input. A cue helps to the extent that it was part of how the item was encoded, not to the extent that it is strongly associated with the item in general.

origin.note: The article "Cue-Dependent Forgetting", volume 62, number 1, pages 74 to 82, carries the subtitle "When we forget something we once knew, it does not necessarily mean that the memory trace has been lost; it may only be inaccessible". It gathers three experimental demonstrations under one heading rather than reporting new data, and Tulving notes it is an updated version of a paper read at the 19th International Congress of Psychology in London in 1969. The pair of terms is older than the article: Tulving and Psotka, writing in 1971, attribute "trace-dependent" and "cue-dependent" forgetting to Tulving and Madigan (1970).

evidence: Three paradigms carry the case, and all three are Tulving's. Tulving and Pearlstone gave 929 high-school students a single presentation of a categorised word list, then tested recall with or without the category names printed on the answer sheet. Cued recall beat uncued recall on all nine lists, and the gap grew with list length. For the 48-word list with one item per category the difference was 19.8 items, or 126 per cent. Subjects first tested without cues were then tested again with them, and their scores rose on eight of the nine lists, though on no list did they reach the level of the groups cued from the start. Tulving and Psotka then applied the idea to retroactive interference. Subjects learned between one and six categorised 24-word lists, and free recall of a given list fell from about 70 per cent of its words when nothing followed it to under 30 per cent when three or more lists did. Handing subjects the category names removed almost all of that. Mean cued recall was 18.0 words for the last list learned and 17.6 for lists that had been followed by interpolated learning, against 15.7 and 11.1 for the same two classes of list in free recall. The third demonstration is the strangest. Tulving and Thomson had 40 subjects study 24 pairs such as glue-CHAIR, remembering only the capitalised word. Subjects then free-associated to strong extralist cues such as table, and among their responses were on average 17.7 of the 24 targets, 74 per cent of them. Asked to circle the words they recognised from the study list, they got 24 per cent, with 4.5 per cent false positives. Given the original input cues instead, they recalled 63 per cent. Experiment 2 repeated it with 22 subjects: 22 per cent recognition against 59 per cent cued recall. Subjects were producing the target word, failing to identify it as the studied word, and then recalling it when the pair mate was restored.

replication.headline: Recognition failure of recallable words fitted one curve across 40 conditions in 12 experiments and kept turning up for two decades after, and the dispute is over what produces it rather than whether it happens.
replication.detail: Tulving and Wiseman pooled 40 experimental conditions from 12 experiments and plotted the probability of recognising a word, given that it was later recalled, against the overall recognition hit rate. The points fell close to one curve. Their fitted equation used a single constant set at .50, the correlation between observed and predicted points was .95, and the standard error of estimate was .028. Their conclusion was that recognition failure "always occurs whenever recognition is imperfect". Nilsson and Gardiner later assembled a database of the relevant conditions published between 1973 and 1992, and Gardiner and Nilsson describe it as 301 observations. Their title is about the exceptions, so the curve is not universal, and the effect it describes recurs across the two decades the database covers. What the function means is another matter. Hintzman argued that data points approach the curve because they are mathematically constrained to, and that the exceptions are the points least subject to that constraint. Gardiner and Nilsson answered with the database and concluded that mathematical constraints have only a minor influence, not the causal role Hintzman's model assigns them. Tulving and Flexser replied to Hintzman in the same issue of Psychological Review. Lian, Glass and Raanaas re-analysed the same database, found recognition given recall rose with recognition and fell with recall, and reported that in their own experiments recognition failure appeared only for items whose names shared three or more opening letters. Their conclusion was that the function is an artefact of collapsing across items. The most recent challenge is to the interpretation rather than the arithmetic. Ozubko, Sirianni, Ahmad, MacLeod and Addante ran five experiments with event-related potentials and found that recalled words that were later recognised showed recollection at recall, while recognition failures did not, and may instead reflect semantic priming. The cue reinstatement branch of the idea has its own modern estimate. Symeonidou, Emmer, Wulff and Kuhlmann pooled 106 effect sizes from 33 studies and 2,177 participants and put the context reinstatement effect at Hedges' g = 0.32, with no difference between younger and older adults.

study.cite: Nilsson, L.-G., & Gardiner, J. M. (1993). Identifying exceptions in a database of recognition failure studies from 1973 to 1992. Memory & Cognition, 21(3), 397-410.

limits: The strongest objection to the idea came from Tulving. Listing criticisms of his own hypothesis in 1974, he wrote that the complaint that it cannot be refuted is a serious one and that "the validity of this criticism must be conceded". He kept the hypothesis as a guide to theory rather than as a claim that data could overturn. He also conceded that the supporting experiments occupy a narrow domain, and that it would be unreasonable to claim the hypothesis applies to all forgetting. The famous 63 per cent cued recall figure in Tulving and Thomson's Experiment 1 rests on 10 subjects. The fifth task was added after 30 subjects had already been run, so the 24 per cent recognition rate comes from 40 people and the recall figure it is set against comes from a quarter of them. Experiment 2 tested the comparison within all 22 subjects and got 22 against 59 per cent. Nilsson and Gardiner's paper is paywalled; only its abstract was read here, and the count of 301 observations is taken from Gardiner and Nilsson's own later description of the database rather than from the database paper. Hintzman's 1992 argument and Tulving and Flexser's reply are both paywalled, and Hintzman's claim is described here from Gardiner and Nilsson's summary of it. The 1974 article carries no DOI and is cited here from a scanned copy on Endel Tulving's publication archive. Symeonidou and colleagues' abstract reports g = 0.32 without an interval, and none is quoted. No preregistered multi-laboratory replication of the recognition failure paradigm was located in searches of Crossref, PubMed and the open web.
misreadings: The hypothesis does not say that memories are permanent. Tulving dealt with that reading directly, calling it a straw man, and wrote that a retrieval environment needed to recover a given trace may never be recreated, so permanent forgetting sits inside the theory rather than outside it. Nor does it say that retrieval cues are themselves remembered or forgotten. Tulving compares retrieval information to the light by which a page is read, and nobody treats darkness as a failure of perception. Recognition failure is also not the general claim that recall beats recognition. Tulving and Wiseman note that Reder, Anderson and Bjork reversed the recall advantage using low-frequency words, and that eight of their own 40 data points come from an experiment in which recall was lower than recognition throughout, yet fit the same function. Cueing does not restore everything either. In Tulving and Pearlstone the subjects tested first without cues improved when the category names arrived, and on none of the nine lists did they catch the groups that had the cues all along. The last confusion is with the environmental version of the idea. Cue-dependent forgetting is a claim about retrieval information of any kind, and changing rooms is one small case of it, covered here under state-dependent memory. Smith and Vela note that direct experimental comparisons, including Godden and Baddeley's underwater work and Smith, Glenberg and Bjork, found environmental context affecting recall and not recognition. Tulving's recognition failure runs the other way, which is worth holding in mind before treating the two literatures as one.
